payload.text: Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026. The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data , already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor. With co-founder Jensen Huang ’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China , we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold. A widening investment footprint Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall. Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year , when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior. The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI ’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic ’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.) The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI . Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion. Beyond the biggest AI labs NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers. The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI ’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi ’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics , which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc . As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data. For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers. The question of what comes next Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter. Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership. payload.text: In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition. In reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat. Fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week , both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat. The looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test. The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception. Our findings below: No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert : Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor. That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food. Made by: Medici Brands ( David parent company). No. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda : The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can. But what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein. Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit) No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn : Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving. Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose. Made by: Khloud No. 4 Mosh : In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he launched with his mother, Maria Shriver . The Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not. I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure. Made by: Mosh No. 5 Cadootz Crackers : We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed. For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor. As someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well. Made by: Cadootz! No. 6 Frozen One : For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint. Yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s . But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job. Made by: Frozen One No. 7 Brami Protein Pasta : We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber. With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich. Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture issues. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami. Made by: Brami Related Crunchbase query: Protein Snacks And Packaged Foods Startups Related reading: VCs Are Still Chasing Protein, Even As Fake Meat Falls Out Of Favor Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: By Yakov Filippenko One day, I woke up to a notice that our app had been removed from Apple’s App Store. For the next month or so, we racked our brains trying to find out why. We even reached out to our internal contacts, only for them to tell us that helping us could put their jobs at risk. Nothing seemed to work. For years, the App Store’s unwritten contract seemed simple. As long as you followed the guidelines, your storefront would remain available. Then a removal notice arrives, and you wonder whether your business can survive. In 2025, Apple removed 166,899 apps and reported just 423 restorations after appeals. As we learned, being caught in it feels like watching your business collapse, with no guarantee of recovery. It’s not all bad news, though. We survived, and this episode taught me that platform dependency is ultimately infrastructure risk. As founders, we prepare for cloud outages and payment failures, but losing access to the platform that brings us customers deserves the same attention. Fortunately, we were prepared, and this is how you can be, too. Understand what a removal can take away Yakov Filippenko, founder and CEO at Intch. First, prospective customers can no longer download your app. Then, paying subscribers flood support with a more damaging question. “The app is gone. Are you a scam?” The bloodshed continues as existing users replace their phones and can’t reinstall the app, eroding your customer base. Financially, Apple immediately freezes funds from the previous three months and turns off recurring subscriptions. For a subscription-dependent company, this can send its monthly recurring revenue to zero. Before spending another cent on acquisition, consider what would happen to those customers if your app disappeared tomorrow. Could they still use your product and continue paying you? If the answer is no, every new customer makes your business more dependent on a platform decision you cannot control. Don’t make an appeal your contingency plan Cal AI , reportedly generating $100,000 daily, was pulled without warning and later reappeared. But its reinstatement tells you little about how long your business might wait. In Intch ’s case, the explanation was so generic it told us nothing. We had 30 days to appeal, but the process ended with a canned rejection. Your appeal may succeed, but your business must operate while you wait. Preparing in advance lets you keep going, whatever the outcome. Build the alternative before you need it Our experience was grueling, but fortunately, two years earlier we had decoupled from the App Store by building a web version and making it our primary payment channel. It also let us ship updates 10 times a day while escaping Apple’s predatory commissions. We weren’t the only ones. Pavel Durov , founder of Telegram , has also promoted web access to bypass store restrictions and potential censorship. The lesson is straightforward. Customers need a working alternative before access disappears. Building one only after removal leaves the business exposed while the team races to replace its storefront. We initially feared the user experience would suffer, but that concern proved unfounded. After the removal, every key metric fully recovered. If you share this concern, test it while your app is still available to see whether customers can use and pay for the web version before they must rely on it. Include platform exposure in growth decisions Most founders see the App Store as a distribution channel, but rarely account for how much control it gives Apple over their business. Before investing more in growth, examine how much revenue depends on continued access and what would survive a removal. Know how long the company could survive an unanswered appeal. Investors should ask those questions too, because a growing subscription base deserves closer scrutiny when a single platform decision can interrupt its revenue. That exposure belongs in funding and valuation discussions. Monopolies act in their interests, and if your business falls outside their vision, you may have little say in a decision that could destroy it. You cannot control it, but you can decide whether it has the power to end your company. By building an alternative while your app is still available, you’ve made the wisest choice. Yakov Filippenko is a seasoned entrepreneur with more than 10 years of experience in IT and technologies, as well as scaling businesses internationally. As a product manager at Yandex , he led a team that grew the product’s user base from 500,000 to 1.2 million and secured its entry into the international market. Subsequently, he co-founded SailPlay , which he scaled to 45 countries and eventually exited, after it was acquired by Retail Rocket in 2018. In 2021, Filippenko launched Intch , an AI-powered platform connecting part-time professionals with flexible roles. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Macronutrients don’t have popularity contests. But if they did, protein would surely be this era’s winner. For everything from sodas to snack bars to pasta, it’s now standard practice for food and drink makers to play up protein content whenever feasible. While we may cut carbs and fret over fat, most of us are still keen on protein. Startups and their backers have been riding this trend too. Over the past decade, investors have poured billions into upstarts promising cheaper, tastier and more sustainable ways to meet our protein quotas. Unfortunately, many of their earlier bets have fared poorly. Vast sums poured into lab-grown meat several years ago, for instance, have so far failed to produce a success story. Former high-flying plant-based meat startups Beyond (now public) and Impossible Foods have seen their valuations wither. Others have shuttered. In response, more recent startup investment has shifted away from meat substitutes and toward stuffing more protein into other packaged foods and drinks. It’s a fad that’s obvious on supermarket shelves, where startups and established brands alike relentlessly tout the added protein in their noodles, pancakes, cereals, energy bars, popcorn and so on. Deal flow looks robust In startup circles, protein-related investment looks tiny in comparison to the billions bet on AI. Deal flow, however, remains fairly robust, with Crunchbase identifying a few dozen protein-focused startups funded in the past year. Moreover, some of these rounds are quite sizable, like a $250 million September Series B for Medici Brands , maker of David Protein snack bars. To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together sample sets of recently-funded protein-focused companies across several themes. These include packaged foods, drinks, ingredients and processes, and animal feed. Protein snacks and packaged foods Snacks and packaged foods look like the largest fundraisers among protein startups, securing hundreds of millions in the past year. For a sense of who’s raising, we put together a list of seven recently funded brands that are finding their way to store shelves. The bulk of recent funding went to the aforementioned parent of David Protein. That brand, in addition to churning sweet-flavored bars with a protein content to rival cod , has been expanding into ice cream and milkshakes. Wilde Brands , which makes crackers from chicken breasts, has also proven popular with investors, pulling in $40 million last month. Among early-stage startups, meanwhile, Frozen One has been off to a brisk start, raising over $8 million for a line of high-protein ice creams now selling at Target . Protein drinks Startups and investors are also catering to people who want their high-protein diet in drinkable form. To illustrate, we put together six recently funded examples below. Ripple Foods , which makes a vegan milk using pea protein, is the highest historical funding recipient, raising over $300 million in its 12-year-history, even though it hasn’t officially joined the unicorn club. Clear protein drinks are also increasingly a thing, with multiple startups including protein soda brand Juuz and sports drink purveyor Protein2o . Precision fermentation and plant protein ingredients Quite a few funded startups are focused more on novel, protein-rich ingredients rather than their own branded retail lineup. In many cases, they’re using precision fermentation to deliver. We put together seven examples below. The Every Co. , which makes animal-free egg white proteins through fermentation, is the biggest funding recipient and one of the older names on our list. It’s raised nearly $300 million in the past 10 years, including a $55 million round a year ago. Early stage is also seeing some action from startups including Edonia , which makes a high-protein cooking ingredient from spirulina, Animal feed and pet food A number of funded protein startups are also focusing on pets and livestock — a target audience that’s not quite so overwhelmed by supermarket options. To illustrate, we aggregated five such companies that raised funding in recent quarters. Notably, two of them — InnovaFeed and nextProtein — are bug-focused. InnovaFeed has raised over $500 million to raise insects for feeding livestock, pet food and aquaculture. NextProtein is using fly larvae for feedstock. Others are focused on pets. Meatly , for instance, secured a Series A round this spring to build what it says will be Europe’s largest cultivated meat facility. It plans to partner with pet food brands and sell its own branded lineup once production scales. Broad focus: Protein, not meat If we were to encapsulate a broad trend across most of the protein-related financings it would be that startups aren’t trying to convince people that vegetables are meat. Rather, they’re focused largely on protein as an in-demand macronutrient that can be increasingly concentrated and stuffed into a bewildering variety of flavors and form factors. That might not all taste as good as their more sugary, high-fat and carb-laden alternatives, but at least they’ve got protein. It turned out that Vélez had an opportunity for Echavarria: Nubank was about to announce its expansion into Colombia and hire a launch team. By late 2020, Echavarría had returned home to join it, with plans to eventually start a company of his own. Felipe Monsalve, Cipriano Echavarría and Nicolás Gómez del Campo, founders of Palomma. (Courtesy photo) Now Echavarría’s Medellín-based startup, Palomma , has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Mexican venture firm Cometa to expand its financial services business for landlords, tenants and property managers, Crunchbase News has exclusively learned. The financing brings Palomma’s total funding to $14 million, including $4 million in previously undisclosed funding, according to Echavarría, its co-founder and CEO. Participants include Volpe Capital , Clocktower Technology Ventures , Tekton Ventures , Simma Capital and Yango Ventures , alongside existing investors Y Combinator , 17Sigma , Nido Ventures and Norte Ventures . Palomma says its annual recurring revenue has grown thirtyfold in 18 months to about $3 million. It processes about $130 million in monthly rental payments, serving more than 200,000 tenants through over 500 property managers in Colombia. It estimates $1.5 billion in annualized rent payment volume. The company will use the funding to expand in Colombia, develop additional AI and financial products, and prepare to enter other markets. It is considering Mexico, Brazil and the Spanish-speaking U.S. market, although Echavarría said Colombia remains the priority. “We want to win Colombia,” he said in an interview. Finding a business in rent payments Palomma’s business combines software that helps property managers handle leasing inquiries, customer service and collections with a payments system for collecting rent and paying landlords. Those relationships let it sell financing, rental guarantees, and other financial products to tenants and property owners. After nearly two years at Nubank, Echavarría went on to found Palomma with Felipe Monsalve and Nicolás Gómez del Campo , MIT -trained engineers with experience at Meta , Cobre and JP Morgan . The founders entered Y Combinator in January 2023 intending to build an account-to-account payments processor for Spanish-speaking Latin America. Growth was largely flat during the first year, Echavarría said. But then property managers began asking for help collecting rent. It soon became apparent that there were problems on both sides of the transaction. Tenants paid rent early in the month, but got their paychecks in twice-monthly installments. Meanwhile, landlords depended on rental income but struggled to borrow against it or protect themselves when tenants stopped paying. Property managers handled collections and payouts through labor-intensive processes, Echavarría said. Rather than acquire tenants and landlords as customers individually, Palomma decided to reach them through the companies managing their properties. The team decided, “let’s basically use the property managers as a distribution channel,” Echavarría recalled. From software to financial services Property managers get access to Palomma’s AI software, which handles tasks such as leasing conversations. It then offers to process their rent payments. Those payments give the company a record of rental income and tenant payment histories that it can use to assess applicants for financial products. From there, Palomma offers services for both tenants and landlords. Palomma Plus gives tenants rewards and credit-building benefits, while Palomma Advance lets landlords collect up to 12 months of future rental income upfront. Palomma Protect covers rental income if a tenant defaults. The company is also developing Palomma Flex, which would let tenants split their monthly rent into two installments. Property managers pay a subscription fee for the AI software, and Palomma earns a percentage of rent through its payments and financial services. Getting customers to adopt more of its services has helped drive Palomma’s growth. The company reports net revenue retention of 390% after 12 months, meaning revenue from an existing group of customers nearly quadrupled, even after accounting for customers who left or spent less. Overall, the decision to combine AI leasing software, payments and financial services reflects Echavarría’s view of what it takes to build a large business in Latin America. He pointed to U.S. companies such as EliseAI , Bilt , TheGuarantors and Flex as comparisons for different parts of Palomma’s business.  Echavarría believes that reaching a similar scale in Latin America requires a wider range of products. “In the U.S., you can build one solution and be really large because the market allows it,” he said. “In Latin America, if you want to be really large, you need to do all the things.” Managing the risk AI also helps decide which tenants qualify for rental guarantees. Palomma’s leasing agent communicates through WhatsApp and collects application documents. The company claims that it can then deliver an approval in under 30 seconds. The company draws on information from leasing conversations and rental payment behavior to assess applicants. The company’s rental guarantees put Palomma on the hook if tenants don’t pay. The startup initially takes on that risk itself, but Echavarría told Crunchbase News it was working to finalize a partnership with an insurer that would share the risk and let Palomma offer more guarantees. The startup is also using AI to keep its team small. As of Nov. 4, it had 18 employees, up from about 14 when it closed its Series A roughly three weeks earlier. A single customer service employee works alongside AI agents to support the roughly 200,000 tenants paying rent through Palomma’s platform, Echavarría said. The startup operates on the premise that AI can make real estate financial services cheaper to provide, much as mobile technology helped digital banks compete with lenders that maintained large branch networks. Longer term, Palomma also plans to expand beyond rentals into homeowners association payments and residential property transactions. Pepe Bolaños , managing partner at Cometa, said Palomma stood out for its founding team and the opportunity to modernize Latin America’s fragmented rental market. In Colombia alone, nearly 8 million households rent their homes, he noted. “We look for companies tackling markets where outdated processes create an opportunity to build a proprietary data asset that can be leveraged and monetized through AI,” he wrote via email. Bolaños pointed to Echavarría’s experience helping scale Nubank, and Monsalve and del Campo’s technical and financial backgrounds. In roughly 18 months, Palomma grew to process around $130 million in monthly rental payments and serve more than 200,000 tenants with about 14 employees, he said. “That kind of execution is unusual. It convinced us that this team has what it takes to build a much larger business,” he added. Unlike competitors focused on individual services, Palomma combines rent collection, tenant screening and rental guarantees, gathering data throughout the process, Bolaños said. Directly processing payments gives it insight into tenant behavior that can improve underwriting, flag potential defaults and support new financial products, while AI helps automate operations. “We believe the combination of distribution, proprietary payment data and AI gives Palomma a competitive advantage that can become stronger as the company grows,” he said. Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX ’s June debut. An IPO and a private placement The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans. For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering. Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD , Broadcom , Google , Micron Technology , Microsoft , Nvidia and TSMC . Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. Revenue and recent updates Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year. For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this. The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026. As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago. payload.text: By Michael Drapkin and Nathan Mutter Patents can help startups establish competitive advantage, attract investors and protect innovations. But the traditional patent process is expensive, slow and difficult to navigate, particularly for companies with limited resources. Michael Drapkin, founding partner of Landfall IP. AI is changing that equation. General-purpose tools can research existing patents, document inventions and generate drafts that look like patent applications in minutes. Handling the process themselves can seem like an easy way for founders to save money. But AI’s capabilities are jagged. AI can perform some tasks remarkably well while missing legal and strategic issues that determine a patent’s commercial value. An application can look sophisticated while providing little meaningful protection. For example, a patent’s claims define its legal boundaries and what you can stop competitors from doing. Mistakes involving claim scope may remain hidden until an investor, acquirer or competitor scrutinizes the company’s intellectual property. Nathan Mutter, managing partner and founder of Landfall IP. The question isn’t whether startups should use AI. It’s how much founders can safely do themselves and when legal expertise becomes essential. Where AI can help startups save time and money Founders can use AI to organize technical documentation, summarize existing patents and identify potentially relevant prior art. Turning engineering notes into an organized invention disclosure, for example, can reduce preparation costs and help counsel focus on strategy. But the opportunity extends beyond DIY. The right counsel can orchestrate AI across the workflow, coordinating invention discovery, drafting, drawings and quality checks. AI can help counsel explore alternative implementations with the inventors, identify disclosure gaps and check support for claims. Attorneys can direct that work, evaluate the results and connect each step to best protect business needs. That combination can produce more comprehensive applications with substantially greater efficiency. It is fundamentally different from generating an application with a chatbot and asking a lawyer to review it afterward. When DIY patent filing becomes a liability Incomplete provisional applications. A provisional’s early filing date is only as useful as its disclosure. Later claims receive that date only if the provisional adequately describes and enables the claimed invention. A DIY draft may omit technical details, alternatives and variations essential to future claims. Adding those details later cannot repair the original disclosure retroactively. Premature disclosure. Pitching investors, demonstrating products or announcing innovations before filing can jeopardize patent rights, particularly internationally. Public disclosure can also destroy trade secret protection. Sharing confidential invention details with AI tools without evaluating their data practices creates additional risks. Unclear ownership. Paying an employee or contractor does not substitute for securing appropriate invention assignments. Secure those agreements when people join, rather than waiting for diligence to expose gaps. Founders should also assign relevant work to the company and verify obligations to prior employers or universities. Ownership gaps can derail fundraising or acquisitions. The cheapest filing option is not necessarily the most economical. A poorly prepared application can create false confidence while leaving valuable innovations exposed. When legal counsel matters Counsel can help decide what to patent versus maintain as a trade secret, prioritize filings within the company’s budget and assess deadlines before disclosure or filing limits the available options. An internal process that competitors cannot observe or reverse engineer, for example, may be better kept as a trade secret. Claim scope requires particular judgment. A fraud detection claim tied to one algorithm may leave competitors free to deliver the same functionality using another. Overly broad claims may overlap with existing technology. Valuable claims target what competitors must do to compete. Ideally, a single identifiable competitor can infringe them, and that infringement can be detected and proven. The specification must describe alternatives and variations that support broader claims later without unnecessarily limiting their scope. AI can assist, but strategic judgment must guide the work. Why investors look beyond ‘patent pending’ Filing volume says little about commercial value. Investors and acquirers will look beyond the number of pending applications to ask: Do you own it? They want signed assignments from relevant founders, employees and contractors, with no competing claim from a prior employer or university. Does it protect your moat? The claims should cover what the business depends on, not a feature it will abandon next year, and the application must contain enough detail to support them. Can you enforce it? The claims should be difficult to design around, and infringement should be something you can realistically detect and prove. Making patent protection more accessible AI’s greatest value is not simply generating more applications at lower costs. It is making meaningful protection more accessible without sacrificing legal judgment. Founders should ask how a firm coordinates its AI tools and legal expertise, not simply whether it uses AI. The answer should explain how that process improves both efficiency and substance. Ultimately, the most expensive patent mistake may be discovering too late that a DIY application never adequately protected the innovation on which the business was built. Related Crunchbase query: Global Legal And Legal Tech Startup Funding In 2026 Michael Drapkin is a founding partner of Landfall IP , an AI-native patent law firm based in Boulder, Colorado. He previously founded one of the largest electronics and computer patent prosecution practices in the U.S. at an Am Law 100 firm and was named U.S. Patent Practitioner of the Year by Managing IP in 2022. Nathan Mutter is managing partner and founder of Landfall IP, an AI-Native law firm. He has served as top outside counsel at Oura , Coinbase , Rubrik , Salesforce 1 and many others. Mutter pioneered the creation of automation systems and tools that enhance efficiency across all aspects of legal services. His clients include both startups and large public companies. title: Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut
summary: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows. The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales. Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.) That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.

payload.text: More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows. The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales. Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.) That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses. The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023. At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals. “On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan , a partner at Scale Venture Partners , which primarily leads Series A and B rounds. This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest. Go big and early — or wait Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said. With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said. Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.” Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said. The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund. “We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.” Deals sizes trend higher At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025. Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said. Raising a large Series A For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through. “If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures , whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year. “I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders. She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said. But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.” Related Crunchbase queries: US Series A Funding, 2026 US Series B Funding, 2026 Related reading: Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year Illustration: Dom Guzman

title: Isometric SF
summary: A pixel-art map of the SF Bay Area

extra.author: juscha1
extra.original_title: Show HN: Isometric SF – A pixel-art map of the SF Bay Area

story_text.value:
Technical Write-up: https://www.justinchavez.com/blog/isometric-sf-how/

Hi HN! Showcasing this fun project. I took 1300 square miles of the SF Bay Area from Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles and transformed them into a cohesive pixel map. It's really fun to explore and stumble upon various famous landmarks like Apple Park, Palace of Fine Arts, or UC Berkeley.

The technicals involve using Nano Banana 2 to train a Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 LoRA which is used to prototype the style and generation methods. For final map I used Qwen to train a Klein 4B LoRA which reproduced the style at 1/4 of the cost. More details in the blog post.

Let me know what you think! I really enjoyed this process of fine-tuning smaller open source models.

If I did the map with Nano Banana 2 it would have cost around 7k USD!

Credit for the idea goes to Isometric NYC.

title: Langfuse AI Gateway
summary: open source rust gateway to trace every LLM call

extra.author: clemo_ra
extra.original_title: Show HN: Langfuse AI Gateway, open source rust gateway to trace every LLM call

story_text.value:
Hi HN, this is Max, Marc and Clemens, co-founders of Langfuse, the open source tool for agent & observability & evals (https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse).

It’s been a minute since our last Show HN in August 2023 (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37310070) - we’ve been busy building out and serving our tracing & eval pieces over the past years and have been very lucky to build a successful company and open source project around it. Today, we are happy to show the beta of Langfuse AI Gateway: https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse/tree/main/ai-gateway. You may ask, why an AI Gateway as our second product: it’s been one our community’s strongest asks + integration pattern that we’ve seen. We want to offer a scalable, reliable and secure way to solve for the gateway use case in the same way that we’ve done with tracing/evals over the past years. And we’ve recently grown our team with some excellent folks - expect to see more bigger bets from us.

Our observability SDKs currently see the code you instrument. Much of a company's model traffic runs through code that is not or cannot be easily instrumented: coding agents like Pi, Claude Code and Codex, internal tools, scripts etc. Third party gateways are already popular ways to emit traces to Langfuse and we’re happy to now ship one natively.

You change your base URL and your API key. Langfuse AI Gateway forwards the native request with a provider key that does not need to be distributed across the team. Right now, it doesn't translate between APIs, responses are relayed unchanged. This was a conscious decision to ensure stability for gateway users, as translation between e.g. OpenAI responses and Anthropic messages are imperfect and might lead to subtle failures in your agents.

If you pass a traceparent header, the call lands inside your existing Langfuse traces.

You can try by docker composing langfuse up and then on to http://localhost:3000

--

git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git

cd langfuse

docker compose up

--

On Cloud, each call becomes a Langfuse generation with tokens, cost, latency and time to first token. Prompts and outputs are recorded if you opt in. If you self-hosted you can also track nothing, not even metadata.

Some details:

- Written in Rust. Stateless, with no database; it talks only to the Langfuse platform and the providers.

- 22MB Docker image. Under 3ms median overhead with tracing on, 1,000+ concurrent streams on 2 vCPUs.

- MIT licensed. Self-host it with Docker Compose or Helm or use our Cloud version.

- Your provider keys and contracts. We don't resell tokens.

What’s next? - Budget caps per key, user, team

- Custom model aliases and fallbacks

- Guardrails

- PII redaction

- SCIM user provisioning

We’ll be around & looking forward to all questions & comments

You may ask, why an AI Gateway as our second product: it’s been one our community’s strongest asks + integration pattern that we’ve seen. We want to offer a scalable, reliable and secure way to solve for the gateway use case in the same way that we’ve done with tracing/evals over the past years. And we’ve recently grown our team with some excellent folks - expect to see more bigger bets from us.

Our observability SDKs currently see the code you instrument. Much of a company's model traffic runs through code that is not or cannot be easily instrumented: coding agents like Pi, Claude Code and Codex, internal tools, scripts etc. Third party gateways are already popular ways to emit traces to Langfuse and we’re happy to now ship one natively.

You change your base URL and your API key. Langfuse AI Gateway forwards the native request with a provider key that does not need to be distributed across the team. Right now, it doesn't translate between APIs, responses are relayed unchanged. This was a conscious decision to ensure stability for gateway users, as translation between e.g. OpenAI responses and Anthropic messages are imperfect and might lead to subtle failures in your agents.

If you pass a traceparent header, the call lands inside your existing Langfuse traces.

You can try by docker composing langfuse up and then on to http://localhost:3000

--

git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git

cd langfuse

docker compose up

--

On Cloud, each call becomes a Langfuse generation with tokens, cost, latency and time to first token. Prompts and outputs are recorded if you opt in. If you self-hosted you can also track nothing, not even metadata.

Some details:

- Written in Rust. Stateless, with no database; it talks only to the Langfuse platform and the providers.

- 22MB Docker image. Under 3ms median overhead with tracing on, 1,000+ concurrent streams on 2 vCPUs.

- MIT licensed. Self-host it with Docker Compose or Helm or use our Cloud version.

- Your provider keys and contracts. We don't resell tokens.

What’s next? - Budget caps per key, user, team

- Custom model aliases and fallbacks

- Guardrails

- PII redaction

- SCIM user provisioning

We’ll be around & looking forward to all questions & comments

title: KittyBrowser
summary: I built a web browser in your terminal

extra.author: graiz
extra.original_title: Show HN: KittyBrowser, I built a web browser in your terminal

story_text.value:
I'm spending more time in the terminal, and with kitty graphics support now in Ghostty and Rex, I thought a real browser in a coding pane might be possible. It is.

kb drives headless Chrome and draws each frame as pixels, so you get the actual page, not a text approximation.

Key features: - Built in Rust, on headless Chrome - Keyboard shortcuts, mouse clicks, scroll, zoom, find, copy - Frames can go through the terminal itself, so it should work over SSH CLI, MCP and an agent skill, so your coding agent drives the same page you're watching

From its own pane, the agent runs things like: > kb https://news.ycombinator.com/

What I learned: the best way to design a CLI for agents is to watch agents use it. Most of the commands exist because an agent got stuck. I ran multiple agent loops where agents would try to use the documentation, get stuck and itterate on the docs.

Note this project needs a terminal with the kitty graphics protocol (Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm, Rex) and Chrome. Tested on macOS; Linux builds but needs testers. Windows PRs welcome.

cargo install --git https://github.com/graiz/kittybrowser kb news.ycombinator.com

MIT licensed. Feedback welcome.

title: RealtimeVAD
summary: trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech

extra.author: koljab
extra.original_title: Show HN: RealtimeVAD – trading false positives for 110ms earlier end-of-speech

story_text.value:
Hey guys. I recently watched the latency reports for my local voice assistant, which show a waveform plus silero probability for voice activity. I noticed silero lags visibly on the speech off signal.

There had to be a method to get this signal closer to what I felt is optimal. My idea was to use a 10 ms energy detector with a threshold that adapts to environment or room noise. Which worked amazingly well. It created more false positives but in my speculative generation pipeline that would not matter. If it's wrong and the user continues speaking I can abort the pipeline fast.

I benchmarked my solution over ~3200 turns from my assistant logs and it came out ~110 ms faster initially. Still 100 ms now after some a fix which was needed for quiet speech.

I made it public if you want to have a look. If you measure it on your data I really appreciate any feedback. There's a benchmark script in the repo.

Thx for reading, have a good day folks.

title: Cerulion
summary: ROS 2-compatible robotics runtime with multi-process replay

extra.author: lakshays
extra.original_title: Show HN: Cerulion – ROS 2-compatible robotics runtime with multi-process replay

story_text.value:
Hey HN! I'm Lakshay. Raveen and I have built Cerulion, a ROS2-compatible robotics runtime written in Rust. We've worked hard on lowering IPC transport latencies without making the single process tradeoff or forcing POD message types. These fast multi-process graphs can then be resimmed deterministically, and existing ROS2 nodes/launch files can run unmodified alongside native Cerulion Rust/Python code. Installation and quickstart (with a one-shot prompt for your favorite coding agent) here at the repo README: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion

I worked on off-road autonomy during my PhD at MIT, and we kept running into inter-process latency in ROS (2 lidars and 6 cameras). Loaned messages need POD types, which nukes standard, vendor-agnostic Image/PointCloud2. We ended up running some hot paths in a brittle single process, which made debugging a nightmare. I'm sure you've seen the heisenbugs ROS-based stacks can produce, with no way to easily reproduce the consumption order or interleaving of callbacks. Valuable data of runtime failures on the robot was hard to use effectively without deterministic reproducibility.

This is what we fix. Cerulion bags record per-input reads and scheduler traces alongside message content in standard MCAPs. cerulion bag play --resim all --verify re-executes node code on the recorded schedule and compares each byte for exact matches or within defined tolerances. Exit 0 is a match, 1 shows the first topic/frame that diverges, 6 shows schedule divergence and --report gives an optional CI verdict. Eligible ROS2 processes can replay deterministically as well.

Here's the data loop:

1. Run: Dependency-ordered level-based DAG scheduler with periodic/data/sync triggers, I/O deadlines, backpressure, and automatic profiling for process partitioning. Each node by default free-runs in its own process while preserving deterministic replay. Live runs pause/resume, and UMWAIT/WFE parks idle consumers on CPUs that support it. Wall-clock reads and runtime thread spawns in user code rejected at compile time by macros.

ROS 2 is supported with rmw_cerulion for Foxy, Humble, Jazzy and Lyrical, that lets you run ROS2 nodes/launch files unmodified in the same graph as native Cerulion nodes. LD_PRELOAD gives ROS2 code shared memory loans through std::vector/std::string. cerulion ros2 attach folds in already-running ROS2 robots, and cerulion ros2 run/launch lets you run existing ROS2 workspaces on Cerulion without any additional setup (with an optional automatic migrate suggested that rewrites C++ publish sites).

2. Move: iceoryx2 shared memory with no serialization, no payload copy and no payload-sized allocation, including for variable-length messages like sensor_msgs/Image and PointCloud2. Round trip latency for a 1MiB sensor_msgs/Image between two processes is 4.08µs p50, with a tight tail of 7.38µs p99 (under 2x p50), with recording on. This is default Cerulion, against 10.95 ms for default ROS 2 Jazzy. Cerulion's p50 and p99 stay flat from 64B to 16 MiB.

3. Capture: With this round-trip latency, there are no tradeoffs, not for process isolation and not for bagging. We can afford always-on or event-based logging. Flashback is our robot dashcam: keeps ~30s of all logs and message contents in memory and saves it automatically on process crashes, topic stalls or declared incidents/manual triggers.

4. Reach: A free account lets you pair robots and desks, letting all your devices find each other with no config, IP addresses or discovery chatter. Pubsub is authenticated and on-demand, with signed grants that the robot verifies offline. We use Iroh to hole-punch or relay over WAN, and mDNS over LAN to transmit data using QUIC. Remote topics mirror into local shared memory, and each device has a single network gateway.

5. Diagnose: cerulion doctor scans for compile/run-time issues (better than Windows Troubleshooter I promise) and suggests fixes. Hindsight is an early access MCP to let agents analyze your bags.

To get started: go to the repo, install Cerulion with the curl one-liner, and paste the prompt in Claude Code/Codex: https://github.com/cerulion-inc/cerulion#quickstart-run-reco.... Or shift your own gears, it's all in the repo that you should star!

The CLI needs a free account, which we use to make device pairing as easy as AirDrop USED to be ;) Everything runs on Linux (x86_64/ARM64), macOS and Android (JNI), with more platforms coming.

We'd love to hear your feedback! If you run ROS 2 on a real robot, point this at your stack and tell us what breaks.

Docs: https://docs.cerulion.com

Site: https://cerulion.com

title: Kapso
summary: Iterative learning from enterprise data

extra.author: alirezamshi
extra.original_title: Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data

story_text.value:
Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo (https://leeroo.com/). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso (https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run.

The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation.

For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions.

The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox.

We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack.

You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs

Here’s how it works…

Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it. For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject.

After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic.

kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new <name>), and compound over that by running experimentations.

We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results…

- Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model (https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model.

- ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems (https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107).

- AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems (https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re...).

We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia (https://leeroopedia.com/): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents.

If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help!

title: Apron Chat Protocol
summary: Hi HN friends - I've been obsessed with chat protocols for ages - one previous project is ssh-chat ( https://ssh.chat/ ) I come bringing a new kind of chat protocol that I've been working on sinc…

extra.author: shazow
extra.original_title: Show HN: Apron Chat Protocol

story_text.value:
Hi HN friends - I've been obsessed with chat protocols for ages - one previous project is ssh-chat (https://ssh.chat/)

I come bringing a new kind of chat protocol that I've been working on since I spent quite a lot of time exploring the 14 other competing standards we've come up with in the past few decades.

The protocol details are here: https://apron.chat

I'm hoping that Apron will better reflect our needs beyond 2026, which I expect will move more and more toward semi-private chats rather than global social networks.

Come say hi on the live public demo: https://web.apron.chat

Some fun facts:

- The demo server runs in a Cloudflare Durable Worker. It's quite efficient, since it's hibernated except for when a message comes in. Easy to self-host this in the free tier.

- Despite the JSON protocol being intentionally unabbreviated ("message" instead of "msg", etc), a typical Apron session still uses almost half as much bandwidth and messages compared to an equivalent Matrix or XMTP session. This is largely because Apron minimizes the number of roundtrips and state required for common chat scenarios. Also it compresses very nicely!

- The official reference client is a PWA (Apron Web), we also have a TUI, macOS, and an iOS implementation by third party Apron-enjoyers. There's two reference server implementations (Cloudflare worker in TS and a Go implementation), plus a bunch of minimal implementations.

- My favourite fun capability is embedding streaming messages, great for LLM outputs. This can be done just by piping to a curl command, no additional dependencies. There's also a mode for streaming a terminal (by piping something like `script` from util-linux which handles row/col/baud flushing, no special dependencies either). See section 4.8 for details: https://apron.chat/protocol#48-embeds-and-avatars

title: Turri
summary: a coding agent with the power of regenerative software

extra.author: ponoru
extra.original_title: Show HN: Turri – a coding agent with the power of regenerative software

story_text.value:
Coding agents let me move fast. To keep up, I stopped reading the code, and with it I stopped understanding my own software. I lost my sense of engineering along with it. I was still the one accountable for software I didn't understand. No workflow or better model fixed that, so I built turri.

turri is based on Pi and the concept of regenerative software introduced by Chad Fowler. The ability to regenerate the same piece of code multiple times and always get the same results in terms of functionality is called the deletion test and proves that your coding agent completely understands you. The idea is that every time part of the software needs to be changed, you regenerate a new version of the code based on the durable information you have about the system.

The durable system information includes specs, tests, ADRs, and other types of documents, and it is written in ***plain. You write these with the help of an agent, and Turri starts partial regeneration of the software you're changing. You can repeat this process as many times as you want until you're happy with the change you're implementing. The regeneration also includes proofs that the generated code completely conforms to the system knowledge on which it was based (it implements all the tests that are part of the definition and automatically adds additional tests).

You can try this by cloning the repo or by installing it from my landing page. I created a desktop app to improve usability. Currently, it's only suitable for new projects, but I'm working on adding support for existing projects.

I also wrote the full story in case you're interested: https://turri.dev/blog/why-i-built-turri/
